A6_L1.visualTitle: Average particle dash and total store are different thermal stories
A6_L1.visualCaption: The chamber board keeps particle count, average motion, and total store on one frame so temperature is not confused with internal energy.
visualCallouts: Temperature tracks average particle kinetic energy.
Internal energy is the total microscopic store of the whole sample.
Equal temperature does not force equal internal energy.
A6_L1.tryFirst: Keep dash level fixed and double the particle count first. That is the quickest way to expose average-versus-total thinking.
A6_L1.takeaway: Temperature is an average-per-particle story, while internal energy belongs to the whole microscopic store.

A6_L2.visualTitle: Heating cost depends on mass, material, and temperature rise together
A6_L2.visualCaption: The heating-cost board keeps the same energy payment beside different materials and masses so learners can see why equal heating gives different temperature changes.
visualCallouts: Specific heat capacity is energy per kilogram per degree.
Larger mass needs more energy for the same rise.
Larger c also needs more energy for the same rise.
A6_L2.tryFirst: Lock the energy input and change only the level cost. That makes the role of specific heat capacity obvious.
A6_L2.takeaway: Specific heat capacity sets the heating cost per kilogram per degree, so the full bookkeeping must keep m, c, and ΔT together.

A6_L3.lessonTitle: Latent Heat and Change of State
A6_L3.visualTitle: A flat temperature meter can still hide an active state-change payment
A6_L3.visualCaption: The state-change board keeps a flat temperature line beside the growing energy payment so learners stop treating a plateau as zero transfer.
visualCallouts: Latent heat changes state without changing temperature.
The energy goes into particle rearrangement.
A heating plateau can still mean energy is entering.
A6_L3.tryFirst: Watch one temperature plateau while the energy bar keeps growing. That is the key contradiction this lesson resolves.
A6_L3.takeaway: Latent heat is the state-change payment, so constant temperature does not mean zero energy transfer.

A6_L4.lessonTitle: Ideal Gas Law and State Variables
A6_L4.visualTitle: Pressure, volume, amount, and temperature belong to one chamber state story
A6_L4.visualCaption: The chamber-state board keeps wall-hit load, room size, particle amount, and warmth together so the ideal-gas law is read as one balance relation.
visualCallouts: Pressure is a wall-hit effect.
Volume is the room available to the gas.
The ideal-gas law links p, V, n, and T together.
A6_L4.tryFirst: Start by shrinking the chamber at fixed temperature so the wall-hit meaning of pressure stays visible.
A6_L4.takeaway: The ideal-gas law is one chamber-state relation, not a collection of detached symbols.

A6_L5.visualTitle: State graphs compare what is fixed, what changes, and how the path is read
A6_L5.visualCaption: The graph board keeps isothermal, isobaric, and isochoric routes beside the chamber story so each curve or line is tied to a physical condition.
visualCallouts: Each gas-law path depends on a stated fixed quantity.
A graph shape only makes sense when the condition is named.
State diagrams are maps of linked variables, not picture art.
A6_L5.tryFirst: Name the fixed quantity before you describe the graph. That one habit stops most gas-graph confusion.
A6_L5.takeaway: Gas-law graphs only become meaningful when the path is linked to the condition that stays fixed.

A6_L6.visualTitle: Wall hits, random motion, and average speed explain pressure and temperature together
A6_L6.visualCaption: The particle-motion board keeps random motion, wall collisions, and average kinetic energy together so gas pressure is explained from particle dynamics rather than from formula memory.
visualCallouts: Gas particles move randomly between collisions.
Pressure comes from wall collisions.
Higher temperature means larger average kinetic energy.
A6_L6.tryFirst: Watch how often particles strike the wall before you talk about pressure. The collision story is the foundation here.
A6_L6.takeaway: Kinetic theory links gas pressure and temperature back to particle motion, collisions, and average kinetic energy.

A7_L1.lessonTitle: EMF, Terminal PD, and Internal Resistance
A7_L1.visualTitle: Source lift and internal loss must be separated before circuit readings are compared
A7_L1.visualCaption: The source board keeps emf, lost volts, and terminal p.d. on one route so the power source is not treated as an ideal push in every case.
visualCallouts: EMF is the full source lift per charge.
Terminal p.d. is the delivered lift across the external circuit.
Internal resistance causes the lost volts inside the source.
A7_L1.tryFirst: Compare open-circuit and loaded readings before you touch the equation. That makes the source-loss distinction concrete.
A7_L1.takeaway: Terminal p.d. is the source emf minus the internal voltage drop caused by current through internal resistance.

A7_L2.visualTitle: Current splitting and voltage loops need separate conservation stories
A7_L2.visualCaption: The node-platform board keeps current conservation at a junction separate from voltage-loop balance around a closed path.
visualCallouts: Current into a junction equals current out.
Voltage rises and drops balance around a loop.
Kirchhoff work is systematic bookkeeping, not guesswork.
A7_L2.tryFirst: Begin at a junction before you begin a loop. That keeps the two Kirchhoff rules from blending together.
A7_L2.takeaway: Kirchhoff analysis becomes reliable when node-current balance and loop-voltage balance are kept as different checks.

A7_L3.visualTitle: A divider is a shared source drop split across the series route
A7_L3.visualCaption: The divider board keeps one source drop, two series sections, and one tapped output together so the output voltage is read as a fraction of the full supply.
visualCallouts: Potential divider sections share the supply voltage.
The output depends on the resistance ratio.
Loading the divider can change the output.
A7_L3.tryFirst: Use equal resistors first so the half-supply result gives you a clean reference point.
A7_L3.takeaway: A potential divider shares one supply drop across a series path, so the output is set by the resistance ratio.

A7_L4.visualTitle: Capacitance tells how much charge is stored for each volt of potential difference
A7_L4.visualCaption: The storage board keeps charge, voltage, and plate separation language together so capacitance is read as a storage ratio rather than as charge alone.
visualCallouts: Capacitance is charge stored per volt.
A larger capacitance stores more charge for the same voltage.
Geometry and dielectric material affect storage.
A7_L4.tryFirst: Hold voltage fixed and compare stored charge in two capacitors. That isolates what capacitance really measures.
A7_L4.takeaway: Capacitance is the storage ratio linking charge and potential difference, not the charge itself.

A7_L5.visualTitle: The charging curve is a changing-rate story, not a straight-line fill
A7_L5.visualCaption: The RC board keeps capacitor voltage, current, and time on one trace so charging and discharging are read as exponential changes rather than as constant-rate ramps.
visualCallouts: Charging current starts large and then falls.
Capacitor p.d. rises toward the supply during charging.
The time constant sets the response timescale.
A7_L5.tryFirst: Watch current and capacitor p.d. together during the first moments of charging. Their opposite trends are the key pattern.
A7_L5.takeaway: RC behaviour is a changing-rate process governed by the time constant, not a straight-line fill or emptying.

A7_L6.visualTitle: Energy storage depends on charge separation, voltage, and the dielectric medium
A7_L6.visualCaption: The energy-storage board keeps field energy, capacitor geometry, and dielectric effect on one frame so increased capacitance is linked to the physical medium.
visualCallouts: Capacitors store energy in their electric field.
Energy depends on capacitance and voltage.
A dielectric raises capacitance by changing the field response between the plates.
A7_L6.tryFirst: Insert the dielectric before changing the voltage so the material effect and the voltage effect do not blend together.
A7_L6.takeaway: Capacitor energy belongs to the electric field, and dielectric insertion changes storage by increasing capacitance.

A8_L1.visualTitle: The field belongs to the location, while the scout charge only samples it
A8_L1.visualCaption: The slope-map board keeps source charges, local arrows, and the scout charge separate so field is not mistaken for force on one chosen probe.
visualCallouts: Electric field is force per unit positive charge.
A test charge reveals the field without defining it.
Field lines are maps of direction, not literal tracks.
A8_L1.tryFirst: Move the scout while keeping the source fixed. That makes the location-based nature of field easiest to see.
A8_L1.takeaway: Electric field is the location's push-per-charge pattern, while a test charge is only the probe that reveals it.

A8_L2.visualTitle: Terrace height and slope arrows are linked maps, but they are not the same quantity
A8_L2.visualCaption: The terrace board keeps electric potential, potential difference, and equipotential routes beside field arrows so height and push are not collapsed together.
visualCallouts: Potential is energy per unit charge.
Equipotential routes keep the same electric height.
Field lines cross equipotentials at right angles.
A8_L2.tryFirst: Walk one equipotential path before you cross it. That keeps same-height language clear before you discuss field direction.
A8_L2.takeaway: Electric potential is a height map, while electric field is the local slope of that map.

A8_L3.visualTitle: A fixed voltage across a smaller gap gives a steeper electric slope
A8_L3.visualCaption: The plate-gap board keeps voltage drop, gap size, and uniform field arrows together so field strength is read as potential gradient.
visualCallouts: A uniform field has the same size and direction throughout the central gap.
Field strength in the gap is ΔV divided by separation.
Smaller plate spacing means a steeper electric slope at fixed voltage.
A8_L3.tryFirst: Hold the voltage fixed and shrink the gap. That one comparison shows why E = ΔV divided by d is an electric-slope story.
A8_L3.takeaway: Uniform-field strength is the potential drop per unit distance between the plates.

A8_L4.visualTitle: Charge size and separation both control the radial force landscape
A8_L4.visualCaption: The radial-force board keeps source size, separation, and attraction-versus-repulsion together so inverse-square reasoning is read geometrically.
visualCallouts: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Force depends on both charge values.
Force falls with the square of separation.
A8_L4.tryFirst: Change the separation before you change the charge size. That makes the inverse-square effect easier to spot.
A8_L4.takeaway: Coulomb's law is a radial charge-and-distance rule with inverse-square weakening.

A8_L5.lessonTitle: Magnetic Force on Currents and Charges
A8_L5.visualTitle: The magnetic side-kick is perpendicular to both the field and the motion route
A8_L5.visualCaption: The field-weave board keeps field direction, charge or current direction, and sideways force on one frame so magnetic force is not treated as a forward shove.
visualCallouts: Magnetic force acts sideways to the motion and the field.
Reversing current or field reverses the force direction.
A magnetic field steers motion rather than speeding it up along the field.
A8_L5.tryFirst: Keep the field fixed and reverse only the current first. That makes the direction rule easier to see.
A8_L5.takeaway: Magnetic force is a sideways steering effect set by the geometry of field and motion.

A8_L6.lessonTitle: Charged Particle Orbits and Motor Motion
A8_L6.visualTitle: The same sideways magnetic push can bend a particle path or turn a current loop
A8_L6.visualCaption: The orbit-and-coil board keeps circular particle motion and motor turning on one geometry so both are read as consequences of perpendicular magnetic force.
visualCallouts: A magnetic field can bend charged-particle motion into a curved path.
A current loop in a field experiences a turning effect.
Both stories come from the same perpendicular magnetic force idea.
A8_L6.tryFirst: Compare one moving charge and one current loop in the same field before you talk about separate topics. The common geometry matters most.
A8_L6.takeaway: Particle orbits and motor motion are both magnetic-force outcomes built from the same sideways field geometry.

A9_L1.visualTitle: Induction begins when the field-thread through a loop changes
A9_L1.visualCaption: The flux-window board keeps field strength, loop area, tilt, and flux-change timing together so Faraday induction is read as a change story.
visualCallouts: Magnetic flux is field through an area.
Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux linkage.
No change in flux means no induced emf.
A9_L1.tryFirst: Start from a no-change case. That makes it obvious that induction needs changing flux, not just flux being present.
A9_L1.takeaway: Faraday induction depends on how quickly the field-thread through the loop changes.

A9_L2.lessonTitle: Lenz's Law and Direction of Response
A9_L2.visualTitle: The induced response opposes the change that produced it
A9_L2.visualCaption: The opposition board keeps the original flux change and the induced response arrow together so Lenz's law is read as a direction rule with physical meaning.
visualCallouts: The induced effect opposes the change that causes it.
Lenz's law is about direction, not about making the effect vanish.
Energy conservation sits behind the opposition rule.
A9_L2.tryFirst: Name the change first, then name what the loop would need to do to oppose it. That order makes Lenz's law much clearer.
A9_L2.takeaway: Lenz's law sets the induced direction by opposition to the original change in flux.

A9_L3.visualTitle: Repeated flux change turns rotation into an alternating emf
A9_L3.visualCaption: The generator board keeps coil rotation, changing flux linkage, and the alternating output trace on one frame so a.c. is seen as periodic induction.
visualCallouts: A rotating coil changes its flux linkage continuously.
That changing flux induces an emf.
The output alternates because the coil orientation keeps reversing.
A9_L3.tryFirst: Follow one full turn first. The sign change in the emf only makes sense when the orientation reversal is visible.
A9_L3.takeaway: An alternating-current generator turns continuous flux change from rotation into an alternating emf.

A9_L4.visualTitle: Changing flux in one coil drives a linked emf in the second coil
A9_L4.visualCaption: The twin-coil board keeps primary turns, secondary turns, shared core flux, and voltage ratio together so transformer action stays an induction story.
visualCallouts: Transformers need changing current in the primary.
The shared core carries changing magnetic flux.
Voltage ratio follows the turns ratio.
A9_L4.tryFirst: Use equal turns as the first case so the turns-ratio effect has a clean reference point.
A9_L4.takeaway: A transformer is a changing-flux bridge, and its voltage ratio follows the turns ratio.

A9_L5.visualTitle: RMS readings and high-voltage transmission make alternating power practical
A9_L5.visualCaption: The transmission board keeps alternating wave size, rms equivalence, current, and cable loss on one route so power delivery is read quantitatively and physically.
visualCallouts: RMS gives the direct-current-equivalent heating effect of an alternating supply.
For a given power, higher voltage means lower current.
Lower current reduces I squared R transmission losses.
A9_L5.tryFirst: Keep the delivered power fixed and change only the line voltage. That isolates why current and loss change.
A9_L5.takeaway: RMS values connect alternating supplies to heating effect, and high-voltage transmission lowers current and line loss for the same power.

A9_L6.visualTitle: Induced loops inside conductors can heat, brake, or sense depending on the design
A9_L6.visualCaption: The eddy-current board keeps changing flux, local current loops, and application outcomes together so induction uses are traced back to the same physics.
visualCallouts: Changing magnetic flux can drive local circulating currents in conductors.
Eddy currents can cause heating or magnetic damping.
Application design decides whether the effect is useful or unwanted.
A9_L6.tryFirst: Read the local loops before you talk about the device purpose. The loops are the shared mechanism behind every application.
A9_L6.takeaway: Eddy-current applications differ in purpose, but they all come from local induction loops driven by changing flux.

A10_L1.visualTitle: Rare large deflections reveal a tiny dense nucleus inside mostly empty atom space
A10_L1.visualCaption: The scattering board keeps beam paths, foil hits, and deflection angles together so Rutherford-style evidence is read from pattern, not from one dramatic event.
visualCallouts: Most particles pass through with little deflection.
A few large deflections reveal concentrated positive charge and mass.
Scattering evidence supports a tiny dense nucleus.
A10_L1.tryFirst: Read the overall pattern before you focus on one dramatic track. The argument comes from the distribution of outcomes.
A10_L1.takeaway: Scattering evidence points to a tiny dense nucleus because only a small fraction of particles undergo large deflections.

A10_L2.visualTitle: Accelerators prepare beams, and detectors turn invisible events into readable signals
A10_L2.visualCaption: The beamline board keeps acceleration stage, collision region, and detector signatures on one route so particle experiments are read as designed systems.
visualCallouts: Accelerators increase particle energy before collisions or probing.
Detectors convert particle interactions into signals we can record.
Different detector signals reveal different particle properties.
A10_L2.tryFirst: Separate beam preparation from event detection before you name the apparatus. That keeps the system logic clear.
A10_L2.takeaway: Particle experiments need both controlled beam preparation and detector systems that turn events into measurable signals.

A10_L3.visualTitle: Decay equations track number balance, while activity tracks how fast decays happen
A10_L3.visualCaption: The decay ledger keeps nuclide changes, particle emission, and count-rate language together so balancing and activity are not confused.
visualCallouts: Nuclear equations must balance nucleon and proton number.
Activity is the decay rate, measured in becquerels.
Decay process and decay rate are linked but different ideas.
A10_L3.tryFirst: Balance the equation before you talk about activity. One tells you what changes, the other tells you how quickly.
A10_L3.takeaway: Decay equations show what changes in the nucleus, while activity measures how fast those decays are happening.

A10_L4.visualTitle: A tighter nucleus has more binding credit and less total mass stamp
A10_L4.visualCaption: The binding-credit board keeps separated nucleons, bound nucleus, and mass-defect energy together so nuclear stability is read from energy bookkeeping.
visualCallouts: Binding energy is the energy needed to separate the nucleus completely.
Mass defect is the missing mass compared with free nucleons.
ΔE = Δmc² links that mass difference to energy.
A10_L4.tryFirst: Start from the separated nucleons. That makes the meaning of missing mass much easier to trust.
A10_L4.takeaway: Binding energy and mass defect are two views of the same nuclear credit: tighter binding means lower mass and more released energy.

A10_L5.lessonTitle: Fission, Chain Reactions, and Thermal Reactors
A10_L5.visualTitle: Fission can multiply neutron-triggered events, so control matters as much as energy release
A10_L5.visualCaption: The reactor board keeps one fission event, released neutrons, and control features together so chain reaction behaviour is read as a balance problem.
visualCallouts: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into lighter products and released energy.
Released neutrons can trigger further fission events.
A thermal reactor needs moderation and control to keep the chain reaction steady.
A10_L5.tryFirst: Watch one generation of neutrons before you talk about the whole reactor. Chain behaviour begins there.
A10_L5.takeaway: Fission power depends on a controlled neutron chain, so reactor design is about both energy release and stability.

A10_L6.visualTitle: Fusion joins light nuclei, while comparison work asks when one nuclear process is favoured over another
A10_L6.visualCaption: The process-comparison board keeps fusion conditions beside fission and binding-energy language so nuclear reactions are compared by physics, not by buzzwords.
visualCallouts: Fusion joins light nuclei and can release energy if the products are more tightly bound.
Fusion needs very high temperature and confinement conditions.
Fission and fusion should be compared through binding-energy change, fuel, and control conditions.
A10_L6.tryFirst: Start with the entry conditions, not the headline energy claim. That is the clearest difference between fusion and fission.
A10_L6.takeaway: Fusion and fission are best compared through binding-energy change, operating conditions, and control demands.

A11_L1.visualTitle: Field strength and potential are linked maps of the same gravitational landscape
A11_L1.visualCaption: The gravity-landscape board keeps inward field arrows and potential depth on one map so force-per-mass and energy-per-mass are not confused.
visualCallouts: Gravitational field strength is force per unit mass.
Gravitational potential is work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity.
Field and potential are linked but not identical descriptions.
A11_L1.tryFirst: Compare two positions at different radii before you mention equations. The changing map is the core idea.
A11_L1.takeaway: Gravitational field and potential are connected descriptions of one landscape, but one tracks force per mass while the other tracks energy per mass.

A11_L2.visualTitle: Stable orbit is a gravity-turning story, and orbit choice sets what a satellite can observe
A11_L2.visualCaption: The orbit board keeps altitude, period, and observation role together so satellite types are linked to orbital mechanics rather than to labels alone.
visualCallouts: Gravity provides the centripetal pull for satellite motion.
Orbital altitude changes speed and period.
Observation purpose depends on the chosen orbit.
A11_L2.tryFirst: Compare low orbit and geostationary-style orbit side by side before you talk about applications.
A11_L2.takeaway: Satellite behaviour and usefulness both come from gravity-provided orbiting and the altitude chosen for the mission.

A11_L3.lessonTitle: Stellar Spectra and the H-R Story
A11_L3.visualTitle: Spectral clues and H-R position together reveal a star's temperature, luminosity, and stage
A11_L3.visualCaption: The spectrum-and-HR board keeps absorption lines, colour-temperature clues, and H-R placement together so stellar classification becomes a connected story.
visualCallouts: A star's spectrum carries temperature and composition clues.
The H-R diagram compares luminosity with temperature.
Main sequence, giants, and white dwarfs occupy different H-R regions.
A11_L3.tryFirst: Read the spectrum before you name the H-R region. The spectral clue anchors the temperature story first.
A11_L3.takeaway: Stellar spectra and H-R position work together to reveal temperature, luminosity, and evolutionary stage.

A11_L4.lessonTitle: Parallax, Standard Candles, and the Distance Ladder
A11_L4.visualTitle: Different astronomical distances need different rungs on the same ladder
A11_L4.visualCaption: The distance-ladder board keeps parallax geometry, standard-candle brightness logic, and range limits together so distance methods are chosen by scale.
visualCallouts: Parallax works well for relatively nearby stars.
Standard candles use known luminosity to infer distance from apparent brightness.
The distance ladder uses different methods for different scales.
A11_L4.tryFirst: Use the nearby parallax rung first, then ask why it stops being practical. That motivates the ladder idea naturally.
A11_L4.takeaway: Astronomical distance measurement is a ladder because different scales require different evidence methods.

A11_L5.visualTitle: Mass decides which stellar pathway ends in a white dwarf, neutron star, or black hole
A11_L5.visualCaption: The lifecycle board keeps birth cloud, main-sequence life, giant stage, and compact remnant branch together so stellar endings stay mass-dependent.
visualCallouts: Stellar evolution depends strongly on initial mass.
Lower-mass stars can end as white dwarfs.
Massive stars can leave neutron stars or black holes after supernovae.
A11_L5.tryFirst: Compare two starting masses first. The branch difference matters more than memorizing isolated remnant names.
A11_L5.takeaway: Compact objects are mass-dependent stellar endings, not separate disconnected astronomy facts.

A11_L6.lessonTitle: Hubble Expansion, Dark Energy, and Cosmology
A11_L6.visualTitle: Redshift evidence links distant galaxies to an expanding universe story
A11_L6.visualCaption: The cosmology board keeps galaxy distance, recession pattern, and expansion language on one stretch-map so Hubble evidence and modern cosmology stay connected.
visualCallouts: Greater redshift generally means greater recession and greater distance.
Hubble expansion is evidence that space itself is stretching.
Dark energy is used in modern cosmology to describe accelerated expansion.
A11_L6.tryFirst: Compare near and far galaxy spectra first. The distance-redshift trend is the best starting evidence.
A11_L6.takeaway: Cosmology becomes more coherent when galaxy redshift is read as evidence for an expanding universe.
